verses.text: Solomon made an alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh’s daughter, and brought her into David’s city, until he had finished building his own house, Yahweh’s house, and the wall around Jerusalem.
However the people sacrificed in the high places, because there was not yet a house built for Yahweh’s name.
Solomon loved Yahweh, walking in the statutes of David his father; except that he sacrificed and burned incense in the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there; for that was the great high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.
In Gibeon, Yahweh appeared to Solomon in a dream by night; and God said, “Ask for what I should give you.”

Solomon said, “You have shown to your servant David my father great loving kindness, because he walked before you in truth, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart with you. You have kept for him this great loving kindness, that you have given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is today.
Now, Yahweh my God, you have made your servant king instead of David my father. I am just a little child. I don’t know how to go out or come in.
Your servant is among your people which you have chosen, a great people, that can’t be numbered or counted for multitude.
Give your servant therefore an understanding heart to judge your people, that I may discern between good and evil; for who is able to judge this great people of yours?”
This request pleased the Lord, that Solomon had asked this thing.

God said to him, “Because you have asked this thing, and have not asked for yourself long life, nor have you asked for riches for yourself, nor have you asked for the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern justice;
behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a wise and understanding heart; so that there has been no one like you before you, and after you none will arise like you.
I have also given you that which you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that there will not be any among the kings like you for all your days.
If you will walk in my ways, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days.”

Solomon awoke; and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem, and stood before the ark of Yahweh’s covenant, and offered up burnt offerings, offered peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.
Then two women who were prostitutes came to the king, and stood before him.
The one woman said, “Oh, my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house. I delivered a child with her in the house.
The third day after I delivered, this woman delivered also. We were together. There was no stranger with us in the house, just us two in the house.
This woman’s child died in the night, because she lay on it.
She arose at midnight, and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid it in her bosom, and laid her dead child in my bosom.
When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, it was dead; but when I had looked at it in the morning, behold, it was not my son, whom I bore.”

The other woman said, “No; but the living one is my son, and the dead one is your son.” The first one said, “No; but the dead one is your son, and the living one is my son.” Thus they spoke before the king.
Then the king said, “One says, ‘This is my son who lives, and your son is the dead;’ and the other says, ‘No; but your son is the dead one, and my son is the living one.’”
The king said, “Get me a sword.” So they brought a sword before the king.
The king said, “Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.”

Then the woman whose the living child was spoke to the king, for her heart yearned over her son, and she said, “Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and in no way kill him!” But the other said, “He shall be neither mine nor yours. Divide him.”
Then the king answered, “Give her the living child, and definitely do not kill him. She is his mother.”
All Israel heard of the judgment which the king had judged; and they feared the king; for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him, to do justice.

footnotes.content: Solomon is building on a foundation David left—house, temple, walls around Jerusalem. But the very first verse shows him taking Pharaoh's daughter as wife. That's no small detail: he's binding himself to Egypt, the great power of the day. I've learned that power and security often whisper they can solve what only the Lord can.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No temple yet, so the people sacrificed on high places. Not yet, not yet—how much of faithful life is lived in that gap, isn't it? The Lord wasn't offended that they reached for Him where they could. He meets us where we stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon loved the Lord and walked in David's ways. Yet—and it's a real yet—he also sacrificed in the high places. We're not always one thing or the other. The heart can be truly toward Him while the feet still stand in old habits. That honest maybe is closer to my own walk than any neat either-or.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gibeon was the great high place, and Solomon came to offer a thousand burnt offerings. That's not showing off—that's a man who knows he needs the Lord's ear. A thousand offerings at one altar, one night. The extravagance itself is a kind of prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the night, in a dream—the Lord came to him without waiting for the right hour or the right place. He came because Solomon had called out. I've found He shows up most clearly when I've finally stopped trying to reach Him on my own terms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon remembers his father's heart. David walked in truth, righteousness, uprightness—and the Lord kept His kindness with him. Solomon isn't flattering; he's naming something real, something he's watched. To raise children who see God's faithfulness to their parents is one of the great gifts we leave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am just a little child." Solomon is a grown man now, a king with a throne, yet he speaks to the Lord like a child. That's not weakness—that's sight. He sees the gulf between what he must do and what he's able to do, and he kneels in it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His people—uncounted, unnumbered, too great to measure. He's not asking for power or dominion; he's overwhelmed by the responsibility for them. A shepherd's heart speaks here. The weight isn't the throne; it's the souls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An understanding heart to judge—to tell good from evil, right from wrong. That's his one request. Not long life, not riches, not enemies defeated. He asks for wisdom. And I notice: he asks for what he knows only the Lord can give. That's the prayer that moves heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This request pleased the Lord. Not because Solomon was perfect—he wasn't—but because he asked for the right thing, for the reason that opens the door to His blessing. The Lord loves a heart that wants to do right more than it wants power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord recounts what Solomon did not ask for: not long life for himself, not riches, not his enemies' lives. He rehearses the refusals as much as the ask. Sometimes what we don't ask for reveals who we really are. Solomon's no-asks told God everything He needed to know about the yes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A wise and understanding heart unmatched before or after—singular, without peer. The Lord doesn't just give wisdom; He gives abundance. And notice: no one like him before him—David, Abraham, Moses—and none will arise like him after. That's the measure of his gift. Yet wisdom itself doesn't save the soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I have also given you that which you have not asked—riches and honor. When we seek the kingdom first, the other things are added. Solomon asked for one thing and received it pressed down, shaken together, running over. Grace doesn't bargain; it overflows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But there's a condition: if you walk in my ways, keep my statutes and commandments as David did, then I will lengthen your days. The gift comes with a door. Solomon will choose later to step through other doors, and the promise will become a warning. Faithfulness keeps us in the blessing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He woke. It was a dream. And immediately he went to Jerusalem, stood before the ark, and offered—burnt offerings and peace offerings, then a feast. No hesitation, no wondering if it was real. When the Lord speaks, the response is worship. Everything else flows from there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two women who were prostitutes came to the king. Not the people he expected to see, perhaps, yet they're here, and they have nowhere else to go. The lowest often find in a king's court what they can't find anywhere else: a hearing, a chance at justice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One woman begins her story: "I and this woman dwell in one house. I delivered a child with her in the house." Just two of them, alone together, and now both claim a living child. In a room with no witnesses but God, the truth is somewhere, buried deep. The Lord sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We were together. There was no stranger with us in the house, just us two in the house. She's setting the stage: no one to corroborate, no one to contradict. The isolation of two women alone together—the kind of loneliness that makes truth hard to see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This woman's child died in the night, because she lay on it. She speaks the hard part first, owning her grief and her failure. The Lord hears a mother's guilt laid bare. There's something honest in confessing what went wrong before we fight for what's right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She arose at midnight, and took my son from beside me while I slept. That image haunts—a mother's hand reaching in the dark, taking a child that wasn't hers, leaving a dead one in its place. Despair moves people to desperate things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, it was dead. That moment—the moment a mother discovers—contains all the dark a human heart can hold. But then: "But when I had looked at it in the morning, behold, it was not my son, whom I bore." She knows. Somehow, a mother knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The other woman said, "No; but the living one is my son, and the dead one is your son." And the first one said, "No; but the dead one is your son, and the living one is my son." Each speaks what she needs to be true, what her heart has chosen to believe. Before Solomon sits the collision of two absolutes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king recites both claims back to them. One says this, one says that. And the room hangs in silence. Sometimes a judge's first job is to name what's true in public—that this is impossible to untangle by words alone, by claims and counterclaims. The Lord sees deeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king said, "Get me a sword." And they brought it. Everyone in the room knows what that sword means. But Solomon isn't reaching for judgment by force; he's reaching for truth. Sometimes we have to name the worst before the best can be born.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other. It's unthinkable. Yet Solomon speaks it as though it's already decided. In that moment, the sword itself becomes a mirror. Only a mother's love moves faster than steel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then the woman whose the living child was spoke to the king, for her heart yearned over her son. Her love cries out before her mind can calculate. She chooses to lose him—to give him to the other woman—rather than see him destroyed. That's the voice of true mother-love, and the king hears it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king answered, "Give her the living child, and definitely do not kill him. She is his mother." Solomon's judgment is plain and swift. He doesn't award the child because she claimed him; he awards the child because she loved him more than her own claim. That's wisdom: seeing what only the heart knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All Israel heard of the judgment which the king had judged; and they feared the king; for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him, to do justice. Readers today hear an echo in this—when justice reaches beyond law into mercy, when a judge sees the soul behind the claim, people take notice. We're still looking for that wisdom in those who lead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
